incidents.inputs: A new preflight script whose whole purpose is to read a project's incident register before delivery, and an outside workshop that had translated the kit's folder names into its own language.
incidents.error: The register path was hardcoded to source/quality/incidents.json. On that workshop the script announced 'this project has logged no incidents yet' over a register holding 109 of them, and its checklist silently dropped every lesson that workshop had already paid for.
incidents.why: Two defects stacked. The path was assumed rather than resolved, and — worse — a failure to READ the file was rendered with the same sentence as a file that was read and found empty. 'Nothing to do' and 'nothing seen' produce the same value, and only one of them is good news. The script reproduced, on its first outside run, the exact failure family it was built to catch.
incidents.generic: A tool that reads a project's data must resolve that path rather than assume it, and must never render 'could not read the input' with the same words as 'read the input, it was empty'. A check that reports all-clear when it simply failed to find its input is worse than no check at all.

incidents.inputs: A plain-text email draft for a real recipient, already composed and hard-wrapped, a few lines slightly over the target width.
incidents.error: Ran a script to rewrap it to 78 columns. The script treated each already-wrapped line as a paragraph, so it re-broke every one: orphan words, a hyphenated word split across two lines, and the two-line sign-off folded into one. Done again on a second draft in the same session before the pattern was recognised.
incidents.why: The rewrapper's input model was wrong and untested: it assumed unwrapped paragraphs and got wrapped lines. Reaching for a script felt cheaper than retyping, and the damage was only visible on reading the whole output, which the first run did not do.
incidents.generic: Compose a plain-text message at its final line width from the start. Never post-process the wrapping of prose that is already wrapped: the tool cannot see paragraphs, only lines, and it will break words and collapse structure.

incidents.inputs: A daily scheduled sweep whose own instructions name the Gmail connector as the only path to the work mailbox, and a machine with two Chrome profiles connected, one signed into the work account and one into the owner's personal account.
incidents.error: The funding sweep ran against the personal Chrome profile instead of the work mailbox it is scoped to, reading a mailbox that has nothing to do with that routine.
incidents.why: Two things. A connector-backed task reached for the logged-in browser rather than stopping when the connector path was not taken, which silently changes whose data is read. And the browser was identified by the handle the tooling prints: the connected-browser list assigns display names per connection, so the same deviceId was 'Browser 1' in the morning and 'Browser 2' the same evening. Nothing in the flow ever asked the browser which account it was signed into.

guard.where: docs/failure-modes.md §2; the task's own Règles dures; memory two-gmail-accounts

incidents.generic: A task backed by an API stops and reports when the API fails; it never falls back to the user's logged-in browser to finish, because that changes whose data is being read. And when a browser is the right tool, identify the session by what it is signed into rather than by the label the tooling gives it: those labels are assigned per connection and swap between runs.
